text: Good afternoon and welcome to the January 23rd Legislative Committee, the first meeting of 2026. I want to begin by extending a warm welcome back to our incredible legislative staff who have been in Richmond since the General Assembly convened last Wednesday. They've been working tirelessly to review over 2,000 pieces of legislation to bring us to update and we'll hear today on what is most relevant and important to our county and its residents. I was in Richmond this past Tuesday with our staff meeting with our delegation, and I can tell you that the energy on

the ground was palpable. Governor Spamberger's priorities are closely aligned with ours, and we have a real opportunity to build on that momentum and put it to work for Fairfax County and its residents. In conversation with our delegates, I was reminded that we shared the same goals, to bring home meaningful wins and legislation that matters to our residents. Now is not the time for blame or finger pointing. We have real work to do, and we can only accomplish it by being a county of yes,

a county known for partnership, collaboration, and results. As an overview of today, we will first review specific issues, then we will move into bills for discussion, and finally bills with recommended positions. Opportunities for comment will be after each bill topic for discussion, so please hold comments until after staff presentations. Any additional comments can be directed to Jennifer or myself. I'll now turn it over to Jennifer and our legislative team for today's updates. Well, I hope you're all staying warm and are ready for this weekend.

We also indicated that the governor's budget includes the mandated support for the Water Quality Improvement Fund and allocate some additional funding there. It also provides $43 million for the Stormwater Local Assistance Fund, the SLAF funding.

And in the past, we've been able to take advantage of this funding for some local projects. And then turning to K-12 funding, it's at the bottom of page one. The governor's budget reflects state costs associated with re-benchmarking.

And these are just routine non-policy updates of the costs for the new biennium. And that includes the adjustment to the local composite index. However, it does not include any new funding associated with the JLARC study recommendations.

And as you know, this is a study that found that the state significantly under funds K-12 funding in the budget. The governor also updates the Virginia Retirement System employer contribution rates and reflects some savings from lower rates for Fairfax County public schools.

That actually translates into some expenditure savings for their budget in the amount of $52.2 million for fiscal year 27. The governor's proposed budget also includes funding for the state share of a 2% salary increase in fiscal year 27 and an additional 2% in fiscal year 28 for funded SOQ positions.

FCPS would receive just $13 million from the state in fiscal year 27, which is just a small portion of the total cost to provide those salary increases. The total cost is $63 million approximately, and after accounting for the state share, the net cost to FCPS would be about $50 million. So the split is 20% state, 80% local dollars for those salary increases.

And then towards the bottom of page 2, we have a summary for the overall impact of the governor's budget on FCPS. It reflects state revenue increase of $71 million as compared to the current fiscal year budget.

And as you know, FCPS presented their fiscal forecast for 27 in the fall. So compared to their fiscal forecast, the governor's budget is an increase of $53.8 million in state revenue. And as I mentioned, there are some expenditure savings as well as a result of the VRS rates, $52.2 million.

So those combined, the revenue increase and expenditure savings, total $106 million additional relative to the fiscal forecast. and did you want me to go over the caboose items or do we finish yes okay can i ask you just a question before we move on to that so the 106 million um since the fiscal forecast um is probably too soon and probably not an appropriate question to ask you but i would just ask our staff to look

we would absorb the extra over the 5%. The conversations has been that they would not be able to absorb going down to 2.5. So, again, that would be a local cost shift. And then the last one is SNAP administrative costs. So this is the portion that came out of H.R. 1, and the cost shift went from 50-50 to 75-25. They've apportioned the state's portion of that so that they aren't going to – that's good news that they're not going to rely on us to fulfill that.

On the other part of that, there was also a little bit of money around technology trying to get that air rate down. What is not reflected in this biennium is the payments that would have to be made for the error rate if our error rate does not fall below 6%.

So that is not included in the budget, but there's been a lot of conversations about both how to get the error rate down as well as the dollars around what will be needed if we do not. And then I'm going to hand it over to Noelle. Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, Noelle Dominguez with Department of Transportation.

The transportation sections are on pages 6 to 8. There is actually not a lot in here for that. So that is the only reason that there is a reduction there. the rest of the budget. Transportation has its own revenue sources, so a lot of these changes are just due to updated projections, and they change every year. All right, so the next topic is our initiatives. So as of today, all the bills are officially on LIS, and so we've got numbers on them. So on page 5, you'll see HB 55, which is our noise abatement monitoring system. That bill passed last year and was vetoed. So we're hoping for success on that. H, and then I'm going to say

this, we have a new style report for bills. And so it's this long one that's legal. What we realized was that in making this look nice, and we did not carry over the categorization buckets. So we're working on that. So just so you know, so we'll call out the page numbers, but the order isn't as nice as it should be, and we're working on that. So on page seven is HB 250, and that's our initiative around expanding park authority to have the same authority as other localities to

ban sex offenders from the facilities. And then on page 12 is HB 1376 and SB 285, and that's the Urban Public-Private Partnership Redevelopment Fund that's carried by our new delegate, Bulova, as opposed to the old delegate, Bulova, who is now the secretary, Bulova.

And then Senator Aird is carrying it in the Senate. Senator Aird did get out of committee, so we're excited about that. But the financing of it is where it got held up last year, and so we're working hard on that. To that end, budget, I just wanted to give an update, too, because there are corresponding budget amendments for the Urban Public Private Partnership Redevelopment Fund.

It is very hard to say those three right in a row every time. So there are two budget amendments in. Again, we did not have time. The budget amendments didn't drop until Thursday. We will do an update on that next week. But I did want to just pull and let you know, Senator Locke has a budget amendment in for that program of $5 million, and Delegate Bulova has it in for $10 million.

So there are the two amendments in on those. Another one of the initiatives that we've done in the last several years has to do with the budget. It is the pay equity for our local finance rules. Again, they had fully funded the comp board positions for Commerce for the Commissioner of Revenue and the Treasurers, and they forgot our section since it's in three separate sections of code.

So we, again, have a budget in there this year to ask for equity in positions, and Senator Bukarski has that one. We also worked with FCPS, and we have budget amendments in for the JLARC recommendation around getting rid of the linear weighted average for teacher salary, and those are carried by Senator Boisco and Delegate Keyes-Gamara.

So now I'm going to turn it over to Noelle and Christine to talk about the regional transit funding. Mr. Chairman, I do not have a handout on regional transit funding yet. There are a lot of bills going out there, so I just wanted to give a broad overview.

we'll come back with more details next week. But essentially, there are three different proposals that have been submitted at this point. We have HB 900 and SB 730. That is Delegate Sullivan and Senator Survelle. Those are what some people are kind of referring to as the big bill. And that has more comprehensive tax reform. It changes what gets the sales tax or what receives a sales tax There is HB 1179 and SB 638, which are Delegate Tran and Senator Eben.

Those are more focused on the SJ28 recommendations. They're a little bit more targeted, though they do both provide substantial funding for transit or transportation statewide, I would say. And then Delegate Watts has HB 978, which I believe, and again, we're still looking through all of these, deals with service delivery fees to both WMATA and the Commonwealth Transportation Fund.

So with all of these going around, and they've all been sent to separate committees because why would this be not complicated, we're doing a deep dive. We're meeting with all of our colleagues who statewide, regional, from all over, and we'll come back with more information next week, I think, with more of a deep dive on what is in which bill and what seems to be moving.

I think at the moment, a lot of people, at least from our region, are like, let's just focus on the end result of a package that addresses our needs and the details will work themselves out. Mr. Chairman, if I might just very briefly, I think, first of all, I think it goes without saying that our position is we support all of those at this stage. And I think we see how things evolve. I do think there will come a point in time where we'll have to take a position on one of them as the superior instrument. I think most of us feel like the bill that Rip Sullivan is carrying is the superior one, but we want to see how things transpire in the weeks ahead.

So I appreciate that we'll get another update next week. But I think in the meantime, our position is we support all of these bills because they're all helpful to transit and most particularly helpful to the issues that we're dealing with at WMATA. And then we'll see where the process takes us. Mr. Chairman. Yeah, Supervisor Alcorn, but I do want to, I don't want to open this up. Like we said at the very beginning, we want to hold questions. So I'll let this one go, but like moving forward, let's just wait.

Okay, the chairman spoke. I thought we were talking. Okay, thank you. I didn't understand the new process. But a couple points just to build on that that I think are really important. Thank you for bringing back the details. But we do, as you pointed out, the difference between the amounts last year and this year are significant because the one-time general funding from the state that went to Metro, that's not being made up any other way than one of these bills. And the other thing I would point out, and we've talked about this, there's also the local money that we have put in from our general fund that goes into that. So I know at

least two of these bills would address that as well. And the last point I would make is Maryland is probably going to be a little later, maybe a year, than us. What I'm hearing is that they're looking at their fix probably closer to 29. So if that happens, I think it's going to be really important, and I've shared this with NVTC staff and Metro staff as well, that there be flexibility in the language, particularly for the first year, to address critical transit needs that

we have in Fairfax County and in the region, in Northern Virginia, to hit some of those things. for example maybe the old Huntington garage that needs to be taken care of so I would encourage you as you're watching this to keep those in mind because this is going to be a big lift and I don't presume anything is going to pass honestly unless we really all come together and work through those details eventually but this is something we'll need to be talking more later once the details are available.

Thank you. Thank you, Supervisor. Let's continue to move on, please. We're not going to ask our questions because there's a strategy here. We're trying to move forward, but there's lots to cover. Mr. Chairman, will we get to ask questions about specific bills, like what was we were just talking about?

We can't just stop every couple of minutes. We're not going to get through it like that. Okay. All right. So as Noel was saying, that there's some tax reform packages in the transit funding. There are also other transit big tax packages. And so we'll keep an eye on that.

Wanted to let you know, as we know, that's a big priority is tax reform. And then as I mentioned, the budget amendments dropped late Wednesday for the Senate and late Thursday for the House. So we'll have more information on those for you next week. And those are the member budget amendments. So just as a reminder, the annual process goes that the governor gives his budget in December, which is the chart we went over.

Then members can submit budget amendments first week of session. Those drop second week of session, which are the ones where I mentioned a couple of. And then the week after crossover, that Sunday, each chamber's budgets drop, which is comprised of member budget amendments.

And then after that, they go into conference, and the last week they come up with a state budget for the General Assembly. So that's kind of the process of that. Again, we'll keep you updated. The only other budget amendment I did want to talk about real quick, just because I picked up on it, was JLARC recommendations.

There is some money in there. There will be more details about kind of the one vehicle they have for that this year. But I did want to let you know that there are some budget amendments around that. And then lastly, we wanted this in this section is to talk about housing as another one of our key priorities. If you have been on LIS at all, or maybe your staff has been looking, there are about 400 to 450 bills dealing with housing and or land use. And so I did not bring those all back for you. What we're proposing instead, and there's a handout in here called

general assembly bills, land use, and housing. And what that is, is our proposed strategy of how to mitigate that as a staff so that we're not bringing you 200 bills every week to talk about. Essentially, the thought is that we're going to break them. And when I say we, I mean the government relations team, and then we're working with the housing task force. And so we're dividing them into topics. And you can see the proposed buckets. Those might flex as we get through the bills or topics come up. But essentially, we're kind of thinking, what are the subject areas that

are really kind of the big areas? And then within those subjects, rating them in a stoplight fashion of red are, this is just a no-go. This is, yellow is, we'd prefer not, but maybe there's some ways we can work with it. And then green is, we either can support it or at least we don't oppose it.

And so those are kind of the categories. On the handout, we did include an example of each of some real bills that are out there. And so this is the way we'll be moving forward if it's the will of the board. This is kind of how what we're proposing to use as a strategy given the volume of bills this year.

Okay, thank you. That's all I have. And, Noelle, if you wouldn't mind, would you say the numbers of each of those bills? Mr. Chairman, Jennifer, I'm guessing you mean the bill number? Yes, the bill numbers. Sorry. HB 900 and SB 730 are the quote-unquote big bill.

Thank you. All right. Seeing no more questions on this, we are going to move on now on Part B, bills to discuss, and I will pass it over again to Jennifer. All right.

So this is where we move on to that nice large chart. So again, I apologize that we weren't able to categorize them, but the majority in this section are actually on photo speed monitoring and violation monitoring systems, which we provided in a separate handout so it's easier for you guys to see.

So we'll go ahead and start with those, as they're the majority of the bills in that section. Mr. Chairman, so there are a lot of camera enforcement bills in Richmond this year again. And some interesting things have happened over the past couple of days.

So we wanted to kind of give you all a summary of what's going on and some recommendations. So first off, we had SB 297 and SB 306, both by delegate, I'm sorry, Senator Peake. And this is the handout, the three-page handout. He has bills to repeal the ability for localities to implement speed camera as well as red light cameras.

I know we've talked with the board about that in the past, how we were given the authority, it was taken away, got it back. So these bills came to Senate Transportation yesterday, and surprisingly, they were reported out. And I think everybody in the room was kind of a little bit surprised when that happened.

We're hearing concerns from various people of how certain localities are implementing programs as well as privacy concerns. So I don't know how long that will last. It was a 6 to 8 or 7 to 8 vote, depending on which ones.

And there were some others that did change, where the revenue went or whether or not certain areas could have speed cameras. The feeling was clear leaving that committee yesterday that there are some concerns with camera programs in general. So we do have both of these listed for oppose.

The historical is HB 306 because the board has historically voted to oppose red light cameras, speed cameras, obviously the same sort of thing. You all do have programs in existence. On the going forward, the next three bills, and I'm going to take them as a pack, HB 994, HB 1220, and on the next page, SB 84.

So what all of these have in common are what we referred to last year as the guardrails. And the guardrails are fairly similar, if not identical. They say what the program revenues will be used for. They talk about how long information can be retained.

They increase the number of signs that require near every camera from one to two and say that for the speed cameras that the sign, one of the signs has to be one of those that tells you how fast you're going. So that being said, I think the writing on the wall is if anything gets through and programs are retained, these guardrails are going to happen. What, however, is concerning beyond that, so Delegate Siebold and Delegate Delaney bills also have language that waive locality sovereign authority in any court proceeding if something happens with these programs. And localities are

very concerned about the language to waive sovereign immunity, I can tell you that much right now. So at the very least, we would recommend proposing to amend or oppose unless amended because that's a definite concern there. The other changes with the bills, Delegate Sebalds does expand the program in a way to allow the placement and operation of speed monitoring devices in safety red zones, which are kind of, you know, that would allow an expansion of the authority. Delegate Delaney's does not really expand the program. It is just the guardrails.

And then going on to the last, the third bill, SB 84, which is Senator Williams-Graves, she also has the guardrails. She does not have the sovereign immunity language, but her bill does, in the same locations already authorized, your school zones, your work zones, your high traffic intersections. It allows the cameras for school crossings, the stop sign school crossing cameras as well. So those are the differences. So again, I'm happy to hear from

the board, but at the very least, I think the sovereign immunity language is extremely problematic. I think guardrails of some sort are going to pass, and then some have some expansion, and some have not. And then we can go on to individual bills too. Okay, so continuing on.

At the bottom of page two, there is SB 684. What this does is it authorizes special conservators of the peace and technicians to help with this. It does, however, also require a DCJS to develop, approve, and make available training course no later than 2027. The reason we are recommending amend is because the way it's written could be inferred that until that training is created, what happens with people currently authorized. So we recommend amending to put a delay in

this provision until the training has been identified. There is a similar bill, SB 59, which did the same, and it actually did put in the delayed enactment yesterday to address those concerns. I am going to pass off the remaining three bills to Christine Prentice, who is our new legislative associate on transportation purposes. Hi, good afternoon, Christine Prentice.
I am the government relations associate for FCCOT. We've got two bills, two additional bills that address summonses by mail, and one of them is very, you know, they each have pluses and minuses.

All of them, starting with HB 311, will require the summons to be changed. So that is an operational difficulty for the police, and there will be more requirements on the police and on any vendors that we choose to use. There's, again, these bills don't go toward the guardrails totally toward the program, but they're very concerned with due process and people understanding
what is happening with the bills. So HB 311, which is on page three, basically our biggest concern is what is the operational effect on the police and on traffic safety enforcement.

And we're thinking about monitoring it because we believe that these bills are going to probably become one bill with additional changes to summonses and other due process things, providing more information to the person, giving them better instructions about how they can appeal. And some other things that are probably going to end up being okay, assuming that there is some grandfathering in and that there's a delay for any additional training that might be required

because it's several of the bills that we've been looking at are requiring the Department of Criminal Justice Services to come up with standardized training. So they're going to need time and then we're going to need time. And the best possible thing that could happen with these bills is that that time is granted to both, all of us. SB 219 is actually really interesting.

It's generally positive in that it will provide for a second summons and then notice to be provided to the DMV. So if the person does not pay the penalties and fees, that they will lose the ability to re-register their vehicle until paid. And the money would go to the locality.

However, there's always a however. It will require monthly reports from DMV in the localities. So again, more guardrails. And there's a couple of other bills with the same type of procedure. And we wanted to bring them to you guys because they generally go under monitor just because we need to be careful about the operational no precedents that they would set. And then the last one is kind

of, is also a good one. And we're thinking that first, you have had historical support for having school bus monitoring video systems. This bill would bring it in line with the other video monitoring systems that are already in use in allowing the retired law enforcement officer to do the certifications, which would free up a serving officer, and this would bring it into conformance with existing law, so we were thinking that this would be something you guys would like to support, and those are all of my bills for today.

Well, thank you so much, and we're going to kick it off and see if Chairman McKay would like to comment first, and then we will start again at the very end and move our way up. Mr. Chairman? Yeah, I mean, obviously on the school board, on the school bus one, that's good news. I would just say on these others, first, Delegate Siebel, Delegate Delaney, did they reach out to our staff, our police, anybody, and consult about shortcomings of our existing guardrails?

We have extensive guardrails in place already. I don't want anyone to think that we have a program that doesn't have guardrails. They're extensive. And so was there outreach done to understand the current program and what these potential changes would mean for it? I would say that nothing in specifics and in discussions with delegation members over the off session, it was portrayed that this is not going after us, but general concerns they've had from other parts of the state potentially.

Yeah, I think it's important for us then to point out to them the challenges some of these would present for our own program. If the idea is to preserve and maybe give us flexibility to potentially expand it in the future, they need to understand what these things will do to the programs that are in the locality they represent that have been put in place successfully and have largely been supported by our community.

Because there's some things in here that just are really problematic. I mean, the sovereign authority is one that you point out, but there's a whole lot of other ones. I mean, I don't know how you would limit the use of photo monitoring devices in work zones when workers are present. I mean, the workers don't switch these on and off.

I mean, there's just a lot of operational problems here, and I think guardrails are good. I think these guardrails would go so far as to impede the ability of our existing program to function at a high level. And I think we should be pointing those things out.

So I would say at this point, we're monitor, seek amendments to these. I think you're right. There will be guardrails passed. The closest those guardrails are to our existing guardrails in our program, the better. And so we need to be spending our time pointing out the distinctions and where those distinctions create problems for us and try to seek to get those things stripped out of the bill or amended so that we don't go backwards here.

Thank you so much, Mr. Chairman. I'm going to start at the end. If I see anyone looking to ask a question, I'm going to go down. Supervisor Palchuk. Thank you.
